title: Knots and lashings for salvaged rope, webbing, cable and straps
summary: Six knots and two lashings cover nearly everything: tying off to a post, a loop that won't slip, adjustable guy lines, a tensioned load, joining two ropes, and binding poles into frames. Use them with salvaged rope, cord, webbing, ratchet straps and steel cable. Load rope to a fifth of its new strength at most, a tenth if it is salvaged or knotted, and never trust rope or straps of unknown history to hold a person.

materials.item: Rope 6–12 mm: polyester, nylon or polypropylene (halyards, docklines, tow ropes)
Cord 3–5 mm: paracord, guy lines, blind cord
Ratchet or cam straps, flat webbing, or car seat belts
Steel cable 3–6 mm with wire-rope clips (3 per eye) and a thimble
Two poles or tubes, about 1.5 m, to practise lashings
Lighter or hot knife to seal synthetic rope ends, or tape for any rope

steps.text: Check every length before you use it: run it through your hands looking for cuts, fuzzy or glazed patches, stiff or crunchy sections, faded colour and chemical stains. Cut out bad sections. Seal synthetic ends by melting them, and tape or whip natural-fibre ends.
steps.warn: Never use salvaged rope, webbing or straps to hold a person's weight, to climb, or to lift anything over people. You can't know what it has been through.

steps.text: Figure-eight stopper, to stop an end pulling through: cross the end over the rope to make a loop, take it round behind the rope, then down through the loop from the front. Pull tight; it looks like an 8.

Bowline, a fixed loop that won't slip and unties after heavy loading: make a small loop in the rope with the end side on top. Pass the end up through it from below, round behind the standing rope, and back down through the small loop. Hold the end against the big loop and pull the standing rope to set it. Leave a tail at least 12 rope widths long and tie a stopper in it.

Round turn and two half hitches, to tie to a post, tree or ring: wrap the end twice round the post, then take it round the standing rope and through itself (one half hitch), and again the same way (two). The turns take the load, so it unties easily afterwards.

Clove hitch, to start and finish lashings or hang a line on a pole: wrap the end round the pole, cross over itself, wrap again, and tuck the end under the second wrap so both ends leave the middle in opposite directions. Add a half hitch if the load swings, because it can slip on its own.

Taut-line hitch, an adjustable loop for guy lines: pass the end round the stake, then make two turns round the standing rope inside the loop, working toward the stake. Make one more turn outside the loop, away from the stake, and tuck it. Slide the knot to tighten; it holds by friction. Add a turn on slippery cord.

Trucker's hitch, to tension a load or ridgeline: tie a fixed loop in the standing rope (a bowline on a bight or a figure-eight loop). Pass the end round the anchor, back up through the loop, and pull down. Pinch it, then tie off with two half hitches below the loop.
steps.warn: It multiplies your pull two to three times: easy to snap old rope or crush what you are tying down. Keep your face out of line with the rope.

steps.text: Sheet bend, to join two ropes, even of different sizes: bend the thicker rope into a U. Pass the thinner end up through the U, round behind both legs, and tuck it under itself, not under the U. Both tails should end on the same side. Go round twice (a double sheet bend) for slippery rope or very different sizes.

Square lashing, to join two poles at right angles: clove hitch on the upright just below the crossbar. Wrap over the crossbar, behind the upright, over the crossbar on the other side and behind the upright again, 3–4 times, tight and side by side. Then make 2–3 frapping turns between the poles round the wraps, pulling hard, and finish with a clove hitch on the crossbar.

Shear lashing, for an A-frame or bipod: lay two poles side by side. Clove hitch on one, wrap both poles 6–8 times without much tension, make two frapping turns between the poles, and clove hitch on the other. Spread the feet apart: the frapping draws the joint tight.

Ratchet straps: thread the loose end up through the slot in the spindle, pull the slack through by hand, then ratchet until there are 2–3 turns of webbing on the spindle, no more. Close the handle flat to lock it. To release, hold the catch and open the handle right out flat. Pad sharp corners with cut hose or cloth.
steps.warn: Check the webbing for cuts and the ratchet for cracks first. A failing strap or hook snaps back hard; keep your face and hands out of its path.

steps.text: Steel cable eyes: bend the cable round a thimble and fit at least three wire-rope clips about 6 cable widths apart. The U-bolt goes on the short dead end and the saddle on the loaded side. Tighten the nuts evenly, load the cable, then tighten them again.
steps.warn: Broken cable strands are like needles and go through skin. Wear gloves and run a rag along the cable to find them.

steps.text: Practise each knot ten times, then with your eyes shut, then in gloves or with cold wet hands. Before any knot takes load, dress it (straighten the turns so nothing crosses) and pull every part tight.

notes:
## The short list

| Job | Knot |
|---|---|
| Stop an end pulling through | Figure-eight stopper |
| Fixed loop that won't slip | Bowline |
| Tie to a post, tree or ring | Round turn and two half hitches |
| Start or finish a lashing | Clove hitch |
| Adjustable guy line | Taut-line hitch |
| Tension a load or ridgeline | Trucker's hitch |
| Join two ropes | Sheet bend (double for slippery rope) |
| Join poles at right angles | Square lashing |
| A-frame, bipod or tripod | Shear lashing |

Learn these well rather than many badly.

## How strong is it?
Typical breaking strength of new rope and cable. Salvaged material can be far weaker; read any label you find.

| Material | New breaking strength |
|---|---|
| Paracord (genuine 550 type) | about 250 kg; cheap copies often under 100 kg |
| Polypropylene rope 6 mm / 10 mm | about 400–600 kg / 1,000–1,500 kg |
| Polyester or nylon rope 6 mm / 10 mm | about 700–900 kg / 1,800–2,500 kg |
| Car seat-belt webbing | over 1,500 kg |
| Ratchet strap, 25 mm / 50 mm | the label's LC (lashing capacity, in daN ≈ kg) is already a safe limit, often 250–2,500 |
| Steel cable 3 mm / 5 mm / 6 mm | about 500–900 kg / 1,500–2,000 kg / 2,000–3,000 kg |

### Safe working load
- New rope, steady load: no more than **one fifth** of the breaking strength.
- Salvaged rope, knotted rope, or a load that jerks or swings: no more than **one tenth**.
- Example: 10 mm polyester, about 2,000 kg new. Steady load on new rope: 400 kg. The same rope salvaged and knotted: 200 kg.
- Knots cut strength by roughly a third to a half. The one-tenth rule already allows for that.
- Wire-rope clips keep about 80% of the cable's strength when fitted right.

## Why never trust unknown rope with a person
- Sunlight weakens synthetic rope from the outside in, and the damage is often invisible.
- Battery acid, fuel and solvents can destroy nylon with no mark you'd notice.
- A rope that was once overloaded or shock-loaded looks the same as a good one.
- A falling person makes a pull many times their body weight. Even a short drop onto stiff rope can reach the strength of a new 6 mm line, and if the rope holds, the jolt can still injure.
- Climbing ropes and harnesses are tested, stretchy and tracked over their life. Salvaged rope is none of those.

If someone has to get up or down, use stairs or a ladder footed by a second person, or don't go.

## Care and mistakes
- Rope running fast over other rope melts through in seconds. Never let a loaded rope saw across another.
- Polypropylene floats and resists rot but is slippery and weakens fastest in sun. Nylon stretches (good for shock loads, bad for ridgelines). Polyester stretches less and handles sun better.
- Store rope dry, out of sunlight and away from batteries and fuel.
- A knot with too short a tail can work loose. Leave 12 rope widths and add a stopper.
- Clove hitches and taut-line hitches can slip on smooth or icy rope. Add a half hitch or an extra turn.
- Fitting wire-rope clips the wrong way round halves their grip: saddle on the loaded side, U-bolt on the dead end.
